cards.explanation: The answer is twice as many men. Jeroboam, Israel's king, draws up 800,000 chosen and mighty men of valor against Abijah's 400,000. Abijah is Judah's king. That's double, friends. When the other side brings two for every one of yours, you don't need a calculator, you just need a long, calm breath.

The answer is that he calls out to Jeroboam and all Israel. Abijah, Judah's king, stands on Mount Zemaraim and says, “Hear me, O Jeroboam and all Israel!” Jeroboam is Israel's king. So Abijah starts with a speech. Standing up high and talking to Jeroboam's 800,000 men takes some nerve, friends.

The answer is the kingship of Israel. Abijah says the LORD, the God of Israel, gave “…the kingship of Israel to David and his descendants forever by a covenant of salt?” David was Israel's king, and Abijah is one of his descendants. So that's where he plants his first flag. He's reminding everybody whose family the throne was given to.

The answer is True. Abijah says Jeroboam son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon son of David, “…rose up and rebelled against his master.” Abijah is reading a man's work history out loud in front of 800,000 people, friends. That's the speech equivalent of pulling out a folder.

The answer is False. He doesn't shrink them at all. Abijah, Judah's king, says to Jeroboam's soldiers, “You are indeed a vast army…” Jeroboam is Israel's king. Abijah looks right at that huge crowd and says so out loud, which tells me he's not afraid of the facts.

The answer is golden calves. Abijah says they have with them “…the golden calves that Jeroboam made for you as gods.” Jeroboam is Israel's king, and Abijah, Judah's king, is calling out what he made. Gods that somebody made, friends. I stamp cookies all day, and nobody bows to them.

The answer is that they drove them out. Abijah asks, “But did you not drive out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites?” So the priests of the LORD got pushed out. Abijah, Judah's king, brings it up in front of Jeroboam and all Israel.

The answer is True. Abijah, Judah's king, says, “…the LORD is our God. We have not forsaken Him…” He says it right after talking about the other side's priests. So he's drawing a line between Judah and Israel. I think he's proud of that line, friends.

The answer is the LORD. Abijah, Judah's king, says the priests present burnt offerings and fragrant incense “…to the LORD…” every morning and every evening. Twice a day, every day. That's a tighter schedule than my oven timer, friends. And all of it is for the LORD.

The answer is to not fight against the LORD. Abijah, Judah's king, says, “…do not fight against the LORD, the God of your fathers, for you will not succeed.” He's speaking to the children of Israel. He's not asking them to fight Judah's army so much as warning them about who stands with Judah. That's a serious way to end a speech, friends.

The answer is around behind Judah to ambush them. Jeroboam, Israel's king, “…had sent troops around to ambush from the rear…” so that “…while he was in front of Judah, the ambush was behind them.” So Judah has Jeroboam in front and an ambush behind, friends. Talk about a plot twist.

The answer is that they cry out to the LORD. When Judah discovers the battle is both before and behind them, “…they cried out to the LORD.” Surrounded on both sides, they call on the LORD. That's the move the text gives us, friends.

The answer is that they raise the battle cry. After the priests blow the trumpets, “…the men of Judah raised the battle cry.” Trumpets first, then the shout. Think of it like a drumroll followed by a whole crowd yelling at once. It's loud, friends, and I love it.

The answer is God. The text says, “And when they raised the cry, God routed Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah.” Jeroboam is Israel's king, and Abijah is Judah's king. The one doing the routing is God Himself. Judah's shout and the trumpets are part of the scene, but the text puts the victory in God's hands.

The answer is five hundred thousand. The text says “…500,000 chosen men of Israel fell slain.” I think this is a heavy part, friends, and it's okay to sit with that. That's a big number of men from Israel's side. Abijah, Judah's king, and his people struck them with a mighty blow.

The answer is that they relied on the LORD. The text says, “…the men of Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers.” That's the reason, plain and simple. Judah had 400,000 men against Israel's 800,000, so it wasn't about the numbers. They trusted the LORD, friends, and the text says that's why they prevailed.

The answer is Bethel. The text says Abijah captured “Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, along with their villages.” Abijah is Judah's king, and he took these from Jeroboam, Israel's king. Bethel leads the list, friends. Three cities, plus their villages, is a good haul.

The answer is False. The text says, “Jeroboam did not again recover his power during the days of Abijah…” Jeroboam is Israel's king, and Abijah is Judah's king. So Jeroboam did not recover his power in Abijah's days, friends.

The answer is True. The text says, “But Abijah grew strong…” Abijah is Judah's king. The verse goes on to say he married fourteen wives and became the father of twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. That's a full house, friends.
